Moles and Mass.intro: The mole is the unit used to count atoms and molecules. Understanding moles allows chemists to calculate the amounts of substances in reactions.

sections.title: The Mole
points: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number)
Molar mass = mass of 1 mole = relative formula mass in grams
Formula: moles = mass ÷ molar mass

callout.label: Triangle Formula
callout.text: Moles = Mass ÷ Mr | Mass = Moles × Mr | Mr = Mass ÷ Moles

sections.title: Relative Formula Mass (Mr)
points: Add up all the relative atomic masses in a formula
Example: H₂O = (2×1) + 16 = 18
Example: CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100

keyTerms.def: The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles
The sum of all relative atomic masses in a formula
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams

examTips: Show working clearly in mole calculations.
Moles = mass ÷ Mr is the most important formula in quantitative chemistry.
commonMistakes: Using mass number instead of relative atomic mass.
Forgetting to multiply by subscripts in formulas (e.g. O₃ = 3 × 16).

Conservation of Mass.intro: In chemical reactions, mass is always conserved — atoms are rearranged but not created or destroyed.

sections.title: Conservation of Mass
points: Total mass of reactants = total mass of products
Atoms are rearranged — none are created or destroyed
If mass appears to change: gas may have escaped (lost) or been absorbed (gained)

callout.label: Example
callout.text: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (balanced: 2 H atoms and 2 Cl atoms on each side)

keyTerms.def: The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products in a reaction
Chemical equation with equal numbers of each atom on both sides

examTips: If mass changes in a reaction, explain why (gas escaping or being taken in).
Always check equations are balanced before using them in calculations.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that if a reaction is in an open container, gas can escape — apparent mass decrease.

Yield and Atom Economy.intro: In real reactions, the actual yield is often less than the theoretical maximum. Atom economy measures how efficiently reactant atoms end up in useful products.

sections.title: Percentage Yield
points: Theoretical yield = maximum possible from calculation
Actual yield < theoretical due to: reversible reactions, losses in filtering/evaporation, side reactions

sections.title: Atom Economy

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: % atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100

points: High atom economy = less waste = more sustainable
Addition reactions have 100% atom economy — only one product
Substitution reactions have lower atom economy

keyTerms.def: The actual yield expressed as a percentage of the theoretical maximum
The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product

examTips: % yield: did we get as much as expected? Atom economy: how efficiently are atoms used?
Greener chemistry = high atom economy AND high percentage yield.
commonMistakes: Confusing % yield (how much we got vs expected) and atom economy (how efficiently atoms are used).

Concentration.intro: Concentration measures how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. It is essential for quantitative chemistry calculations.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³). Also: concentration (g/dm³) = mass ÷ volume

sections.title: Converting Units
points: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre
To convert cm³ to dm³: divide by 1000
More concentrated = more solute in same volume

keyTerms.def: The amount of solute dissolved per unit volume of solution
The substance dissolved in a solvent
The liquid in which a solute dissolves

examTips: Always convert cm³ to dm³ before using in concentration formula.
Concentration in mol/dm³ is most common — learn the formula triangle.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000) before calculating concentration.

Gas Volumes.intro: Gases are measured by volume rather than mass. At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules.

sections.title: Molar Volume of Gas

callout.label: Key Fact
callout.text: At room temperature and pressure (RTP): 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³).

points: Volume of gas = moles × 24 (in dm³) at RTP
Moles of gas = volume ÷ 24 (if volume in dm³)

sections.title: Using Gas Volumes
points: Can compare gas volumes using the ratio of moles in the equation
Example: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl — 1 volume H₂ + 1 volume Cl₂ → 2 volumes HCl

keyTerms.def: The volume occupied by one mole of gas at a given temperature and pressure
Room temperature and pressure — 25°C and 1 atmosphere

examTips: At RTP: 1 mole = 24 dm³ for any gas.
Gas volume ratio = mole ratio from balanced equation.
commonMistakes: Confusing dm³ and cm³ — 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. At RTP, 1 mole = 24 dm³ = 24,000 cm³.
